BootstrapSimulationDemo.heading: Paper introduction
BootstrapSimulationDemo.text:
[Min Dai, Qing Zhang and Qiji Jim Zhu, *Trend Following Trading under a Regime Switching Model* (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1137/090770552) studies when buying into a rising market and selling into a falling market can be optimal under an explicit price model and transaction costs. The journal publication is from 2010, although the Java package retains `dai2011`.

The market switches between hidden bull and bear regimes. The trader observes prices, not the regime itself, and updates a probability of being in the favorable state using a filtering model. Optimal-stopping arguments characterize buy and sell decisions in terms of that information and the cost of trading. Trend following here therefore has a probabilistic economic interpretation rather than being an arbitrary chart signal.

Optimality is conditional on the assumed regime dynamics, calibrated parameters and cost model; it is not a promise about future market returns. The demo's resampling, calibration windows and position-management choices are additional implementation decisions. The model, filtering and trading-cost sections of the original journal article were reviewed.

### How this demo connects to the idea

The main uses Dai2011LongShort and reconstructed paths obtained from sampled log returns. Each scenario has its own market cache, simulator and report. PattonPolitisWhite2009 estimates a block length for dependent resampling; neither a resampled path nor a bootstrap P/L quantile is a new historical observation or a reproduction of the paper’s market test.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Initial cash is 1,000,000; report measures mix SIMPLE information-ratio returns with ABSOLUTE Omega inputs, so their scales differ.

KagiMRBasketSimulationDemo.heading: Paper introduction
KagiMRBasketSimulationDemo.text:
[Alexandre d’Aspremont, *Identifying Small Mean Reverting Portfolios* (2008 author preprint; published 2011)](https://www.di.ens.fr/~aspremon/PDF/MeanRevVec.pdf) asks how to build a mean-reverting basket using only a few assets. A dense basket may look attractive statistically but be expensive and difficult to trade.

The paper uses a vector autoregressive representation and a Box–Tiao predictability ratio as a proxy for mean reversion. Minimizing this ratio seeks combinations whose current variation is less explained by lagged variation. A cardinality restriction limits the number of nonzero holdings. Greedy search and semidefinite relaxations address the resulting sparse optimization problem; regularized estimation can help stabilize its inputs.

Its central tradeoff is between sparsity and the strength of the mean-reversion proxy. Finding a basket does not specify a complete trading strategy or guarantee a profit. Kagi signals, entry and exit policies, sizing and the S&P 500 universe in these demos are separate choices. Sections 2–3 of the author preprint were reviewed.

### How this demo connects to the idea

SimpleMRBasketProvider uses the configured price matrix, covariance penalty, clustering and basket-selection windows. The demo selects the first basket and passes it to KagiMRBasketSimulation for a trading interval. The Kagi simulation and S&P 500 settings are implementation choices; the example does not demonstrate every greedy/semidefinite method in the paper.

MultiPeriodKagiMRStrategyDemo.text:

Elliott2005StrategyDemo1.heading: Paper introduction
Elliott2005StrategyDemo1.text:
[Robert J. Elliott, John van der Hoek and William P. Malcolm, *Pairs trading* (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1080/14697680500149370) treats the spread between related securities as an unobserved mean-reverting Gaussian Markov process measured with additional Gaussian noise. This separates a latent relative-value signal from noisy observations.

The paper's stated contribution is a model for estimating and tracking that spread and using it to motivate pairs-trading decisions. The intuition is to trade a deviation relative to an estimated equilibrium, rather than predict each stock's outright direction. The relationship can nevertheless break down, and spread convergence does not remove execution or financing risk.

This introduction is based on the original publisher abstract and author-institution record; full-text derivations were not available for review. The repository offers several signal customizations. Posterior-state, constant-coefficient and empirical-quantile rules must not be described as identical implementations of the paper.

### How this demo connects to the idea

The active customization uses fixed coefficients (1,-1), a long-term-mean reference and entry/exit settings 0.4/0.25 on XOM/CVX with 50 calibration observations. The posterior-state and cointegration variants are commented alternatives. Selecting different customization changes what “fair spread” means; the class name does not guarantee that the active rule reproduces the paper’s estimator.

EconomicModelStrategyDemo.heading: Related paper introduction
EconomicModelStrategyDemo.text:
[Eugene F. Fama and Kenneth R. French, *Common risk factors in the returns on stocks and bonds* (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(93)90023-5) investigates whether a small set of common risk factors explains shared variation in stock and bond returns. The familiar equity factors are market excess return, size (SMB) and book-to-market value (HML); the paper also considers bond-market factors.

A factor model separates exposure to common factors from the residual specific to each asset. For portfolio construction, this can explain why apparently different assets still carry similar risks. Estimated factor loadings are not automatically return forecasts or profitable trade signals.

This is related context, not a claim that the demo recreates Fama–French portfolios or replicates the 1993 empirical study. The economic and fundamental demos choose their own inputs and estimators. The original publication abstract and [Kenneth French's factor definitions](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html) were checked; the full article was not independently reviewed.

### How this demo connects to the idea

FactorExcessBenchmark, FactorSMB and FactorHML feed EconomicFactorModel, which estimates exposures/premia over the configured trailing window. FactorStrategy then uses a chosen optimizer and diversification layer to rebalance. Factor measurement, database construction and reporting dates must be consistent; financial statement availability dates matter. The code’s factor implementations, universe and optimizer choices define this experiment.

FundamentalModelStrategyDemo.text:

The active FundamentalFactorModel uses FactorSize and FactorGrowth with SIMPLE returns. This differs from EconomicModelStrategyDemo’s market/SMB/HML factor-return specification. FactorStrategyParam supplies rebalance, risk and data-window settings, while the configured accounting dataset supplies characteristics; avoid treating a publication date or revised statement as information available earlier.

Infantino2010ParamAnalysisDemo.heading: Paper introduction
Infantino2010ParamAnalysisDemo.text:
[Leandro R. Infantino and Savion Itzhaki, *Developing high-frequency equities trading models* (MIT MBA thesis, 2010)](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/59122) asks whether common movements across equities can help forecast short-horizon returns. The thesis studies liquid US equities at intraday frequencies, roughly seconds to minutes; it is not a daily moving-average crossover model.

The model uses principal component analysis (PCA) to summarize correlated stock returns with a smaller set of common factors. Regressions relate accumulated past component returns to future accumulated stock returns. This accounts for different stock exposures rather than assuming every stock should follow the same market-average return. The thesis also discusses deciding between mean-reverting and trending behavior.

The useful distinction is between finding common factors, fitting a forecast, and turning that forecast into positions. Evidence of a fitted relationship alone does not establish executable profits after costs. This repository adapts the idea to daily Yahoo data; its observation horizons, universe, sizing and regime settings must be read separately from the thesis. See thesis Sections 2.2–2.4 for the model. The original model sections were reviewed.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Here T=500 is the rolling log-return sample length, k=2 is the retained dimension, N is the filtered IT-stock count, and H=1,21,...,201 is an accumulation/forecast horizon in observations. Regime switching is disabled. SensitivityAnalyzer creates an Infantino2010Strategy per parameter set; synchronized order books supply aligned prices. Infantino2010LongShortConstantValue reads signal.dReturns(), uses fixed per-stock notional and does not automatically invest simulator cash. The configured Commission measure records a statistic; it does not by itself install a broker fee scheme. Search results on the same interval are not holdout validation.

Infantino2010PredictionAnalysisDemo.text:

### How this demo connects to the idea

DynamicInfantino2010PCA receives T=500, k=2 and H=120 by default; N follows setupStocks(). Overlapping H-period observations can be serially dependent; correlation alone does not establish tradable performance.

JanuaryEffectStrategyDemo.heading: Related paper introduction
JanuaryEffectStrategyDemo.text:
[Michael S. Rozeff and William R. Kinney Jr., *Capital market seasonality: The case of stock returns* (1976)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-405X(76)90028-3) reports evidence that average monthly NYSE returns differed across the calendar, with unusually large January returns contributing strongly to the pattern. Its historical sample covers 1904–1974, and the abstract notes an exception in 1929–1940.

That is evidence of a historical seasonal pattern, not a rule that every stock rises in January or a guarantee that the effect survives costs. A calendar strategy still needs an explicit universe, entry and exit dates, sizing, data conventions and an evaluation period.

The paper is related empirical background only. This demo uses its own January-effect policy and dataset; it does not reproduce the paper's sample or statistical tests. The introduction is based on the original publisher abstract, not a full-text replication review.

### How this demo connects to the idea

This is a calendar-rule illustration: schedule daily callbacks, open one unit near year-end and flatten after the configured new-year date. The code does not estimate a seasonal premium or implement a causal explanation of the January effect. It is not presented as a replication of a specific empirical publication.

OULogSpreadCRRASignalDemo.heading: Paper introduction
OULogSpreadCRRASignalDemo.text:
[Jakub W. Jurek and Halla Yang, *Dynamic Portfolio Selection in Arbitrage* (2007 working paper)](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=882536) studies how a finite-horizon investor with non-myopic preferences should allocate to a mean-reverting arbitrage opportunity, such as an equity spread. A statistical dislocation is not a riskless arbitrage: it can widen before it converges.

The key question is position size, not merely whether a spread is above or below its mean. Optimal exposure depends on the investor's preferences, remaining horizon and the modeled opportunity. A dynamic allocation can therefore differ from a fixed-notional threshold rule.

This summary is limited to the author-submitted publication abstract; the full derivation was not independently reviewed. The Java example generates and fits an OU log spread and evaluates a CRRA allocation rule. Inspect its wealth update carefully: it allocates with fixed `W`, so the displayed calculation should not be interpreted as a fully compounded wealth backtest or a replication of every paper assumption.

### How this demo connects to the idea

The demo generates an OU path, fits it with OUFittingMLE and calls OUSpreadCRRASignal.getOptimalAllocation(price, W, tau). gamma is risk aversion, tau is remaining horizon and r*delta is the rate passed to the signal. W stays fixed while W_new records cumulative wealth, so this is not compounding allocation. Fitting and evaluation use the same generated path. The older Kim/Primbs/Boyd reference is related background, not the provenance of the Jurek-named class.

GMA12Demo.heading: Related papers introduction
GMA12Demo.text:
[Knight, Satchell and Tran (1995), *Statistical modelling of asymmetric risk in asset returns*](https://doi.org/10.1080/13504869500000009) motivates modeling positive and negative return behavior separately. In this example, a return process is the input to an analytical trading-rule calculation, rather than a historical portfolio backtest.

A related theoretical reference is [Emmanuel Acar and Stephen Satchell (1997), *A theoretical analysis of trading rules: an application to the moving average case with Markovian returns*](https://doi.org/10.1080/135048697334791). It studies moving-average trading rules under an assumed return process. The general lesson is that a rule's behavior depends on the distribution and serial dependence of returns, not just its moving-average parameters.

The publication abstracts/identities were checked, but the full derivations were not independently reviewed. The Acar–Satchell paper is related literature: an exact equivalence between its assumptions and `GMA12` has not been established. The printed trade quantities are model-based calculations, not realized account performance.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Convert Yahoo adjusted closes to log returns, call KnightSatchellTran1995MLE.fitModel, then construct GMA12. PrHoldingTime(1) and ERRLong() are model-derived quantities, not realized Sharpe ratios or total portfolio returns. Fitting an asymmetric return law does not by itself establish stable out-of-sample trend profitability.

KnightSatchellTran1995MLEDemo.heading: Paper introduction
KnightSatchellTran1995MLEDemo.text:
[J. L. Knight, S. E. Satchell and K. C. Tran, *Statistical modelling of asymmetric risk in asset returns* (1995)](https://doi.org/10.1080/13504869500000009) develops a return-distribution model that treats positive and negative moves differently. The publisher abstract describes scaled gamma distributions for conditional upward and downward returns, allowing asymmetry that a single symmetric normal distribution cannot capture.

The learning objective is to distinguish a probability model for returns from a trading rule. Fitting parameters or generating a plausible sample does not by itself produce a funded investment account. A fitted asymmetric distribution also needs validation on observations not used to estimate it.

This summary relies on the original publisher abstract and verified publication metadata; full-text derivations were not available for review. The library's generator, estimator and reported parameters should be checked against their own API contracts before claiming an exact paper replication.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Generate N=100 returns from KnightSatchellTran1995, fit them with KnightSatchellTran1995MLE.fitModel and compare generating versus fitted parameters. The parameters supplied to the constructor govern the return generator; GMA12 then computes model- based holding-time and long-return statistics. These are analytical/simulation diagnostics without a funded trading account.

Corvalan2005Demo.heading: Paper introduction
Corvalan2005Demo.text:
[Alejandro Corvalán, *Well Diversified Efficient Portfolios* (Central Bank of Chile Working Paper 336, 2005)](https://www.bcentral.cl/contenido/-/details/documento-de-trabajo-n-336) asks why mean–variance portfolios can concentrate in a few assets even when investors want diversification.

The paper argues that treating estimated risk and return as infinitely precise forces an unnecessarily exact choice on the efficient frontier. Allowing a small tolerance around an efficient risk–return point admits many nearly equivalent allocations. A second optimization can then favor diversification within that neighborhood.

The lesson is to separate the selection of a risk–return target from the choice among near-equivalent portfolios. Relaxing the target changes the feasible set; it does not magically improve the estimates. This demo exposes relative return/volatility relaxation parameters and a diversification measure. Their normalization must be read from the library rather than copied directly from a paper tolerance. The original working paper and its two-stage formulation were reviewed; an accessible [original PDF](https://dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/1364447.pdf) is also available.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Corvalan2005 in this example exposes the relaxation settings and chosen diversification measure through library classes. Its documented constraints use relative return/volatility relaxations; check that parameterization rather than substituting a tolerance directly from the paper. Weights, estimated risk and forecast return are optimizer outputs, not a realized account-performance report.

CovarianceComparisonDemo.heading: Related papers introduction
CovarianceComparisonDemo.text:
[Olivier Ledoit and Michael Wolf, *A well-conditioned estimator for large-dimensional covariance matrices* (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0047-259X(03)00096-4) addresses noisy sample covariance estimates, especially when the number of assets is large relative to the observations. Shrinkage combines sample information with a more structured target to reduce estimation error and improve conditioning.

Their later [*Nonlinear shrinkage estimation of large-dimensional covariance matrices* (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1214/12-AOS989) adjusts sample eigenvalues nonlinearly rather than applying one common linear shrinkage rule. These are covariance-estimation methods; a better matrix estimate does not, on its own, specify a trading strategy.

This page provides conceptual background from the original publication abstracts. The demo compares sample covariance with the library's `LedoitWolf2004` and `LedoitWolf2016` implementations. The latter class name alone does not establish which version or numerical procedure exactly matches either reference. Read the invoked API and convergence diagnostics; this run's eigensolver failure prevents a completed comparison.

### How this demo connects to the idea

This example compares estimators; it does not define a stand-alone trading model. Covariance summarizes joint variability of returns, so data frequency, demeaning, sample size and asset ordering affect the optimizer input. Inspect each estimator invoked before interpreting a numerical difference.

Lai2010NPEBModelDemo.heading: Paper introduction
Lai2010NPEBModelDemo.text:
[Tze Leung Lai, Haipeng Xing and Zehao Chen, *Mean–variance portfolio optimization when means and covariances are unknown* (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-AOAS422) addresses a practical weakness of plug-in mean–variance optimization: historical estimates are uncertain, yet a naive optimizer treats them as known.

The paper formulates allocation using predictive return uncertainty and develops a nonparametric empirical Bayes (NPEB) approach with resampling. Conceptually, the investor should account for estimation risk when evaluating an allocation, rather than optimize once using a single estimated mean and covariance matrix. The method is compared with alternative allocation procedures in numerical and empirical examples.

Its conclusions depend on the statistical modeling and resampling design. The Java API retains `Lai2010`, but the cited journal paper is from 2011. Resampler selection, shrinkage, bootstrap count, risk preference and rebalancing are explicit demo choices, not interchangeable settings guaranteed to reproduce the article's tables. Sections 3–4 of the original text were reviewed.

### How this demo connects to the idea

The active configuration uses Lai2010NPEBModel, a long-only MV optimizer, Ledoit–Wolf moments, an AR resampler, 100 bootstraps, lambda=1.4, a one-year calibration window and quarterly rebalancing. These choices adapt the framework; they do not reproduce all models or tables from the article. Follow the template’s data interval and rebalance strategy separately from the CSV exporters.

MarkowitzBigDemo.heading: Paper introduction
MarkowitzBigDemo.text:
[Harry Markowitz, *Portfolio Selection* (1952)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x) explains diversification as a portfolio problem: an asset's risk cannot be judged independently of how its returns move with the other holdings. Expected portfolio return is a weighted mean; portfolio variance depends on the full covariance matrix.

The efficient set contains portfolios for which expected return cannot be improved without accepting more variance, or variance reduced without giving up expected return. An investor selects a tradeoff according to preferences and constraints. Holding many positively correlated assets need not provide much diversification.

The framework assumes the relevant return means and covariances are supplied. In practice, estimates can be unstable and constraints can materially change the answer. A solved optimization is therefore a set of weights under assumptions, not evidence of future outperformance. The original article was reviewed. Rolling calibration, rebalance schedules, costs and the dataset used here belong to the demo, not to the static 1952 formulation.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Benchmarks the optimizer on generated high-dimensional inputs. Its asset count exercises numerical scaling; no historical strategy is simulated, and runtime or feasibility says nothing about out-of-sample returns.

MarkowitzDemo.heading: Paper introduction
MarkowitzDemo.text:
[Harry Markowitz, *Portfolio Selection* (1952)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x) explains diversification as a portfolio problem: an asset's risk cannot be judged independently of how its returns move with the other holdings. Expected portfolio return is a weighted mean; portfolio variance depends on the full covariance matrix.

The efficient set contains portfolios for which expected return cannot be improved without accepting more variance, or variance reduced without giving up expected return. An investor selects a tradeoff according to preferences and constraints. Holding many positively correlated assets need not provide much diversification.

The framework assumes the relevant return means and covariances are supplied. In practice, estimates can be unstable and constraints can materially change the answer. Rolling calibration, rebalance schedules, costs and the dataset used here belong to the demo, not to the static 1952 formulation.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Trades off expected return against covariance-based portfolio risk. The historical optimizer example estimates inputs from Yahoo observations, chooses a risk parameter and computes weights. Mean estimates and covariance uncertainty are not eliminated by solving the quadratic program.

PerformanceOptimizedYahooEODPortfolioDem.heading: Strategy introduction
PerformanceOptimizedYahooEODPortfolioDem.text:
This example searches for a portfolio using a user-defined performance objective. No single original paper has been established for this particular combination of information ratio, profit and drawdown, so it is documented as an application of the library rather than given an invented paper attribution.

The important idea is that a performance statistic can become an optimization target. Normalization coefficients and objective weights determine how conflicting goals are balanced; they are different from the final asset allocation weights. A search can improve its chosen score on the sample without discovering a relationship that persists afterward.

Read this tutorial as a lesson in assembling and evaluating a portfolio-search workflow. To draw an investment conclusion, use independent evaluation data, verify the cost and turnover assumptions, and inspect the actual account path as well as the objective score. The following implementation section identifies the concrete components used here.

### How this demo connects to the idea

This is an application-level search over weighted performance objectives, not a named single- publication model. The template combines information ratio, profit and drawdown with normalization coefficients. Those objective coefficients are not asset allocation weights, and optimizing a backtest statistic can overfit its sample.

PortfolioOptimComparisons1Demo.heading: Related papers introduction
PortfolioOptimComparisons1Demo.text:
This is a comparison of different allocation ideas, rather than an implementation of one paper. [Markowitz (1952), *Portfolio Selection*](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x), balances expected return against covariance-based risk. [Black and Litterman (1992), *Global Portfolio Optimization*](https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Teaching/BA453_2006/Black_Litterman_Global_Portfolio_Optimization_1992.pdf), combines an equilibrium starting point with investor views and uncertainty about those views.

[Corvalán (2005), *Well Diversified Efficient Portfolios*](https://www.bcentral.cl/contenido/-/details/documento-de-trabajo-n-336), seeks diversification among nearly equivalent risk–return allocations. [Lai, Xing and Chen (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-AOAS422) address uncertainty in estimated means and covariances using predictive reasoning and resampling. These approaches answer different questions, so their risk parameters and assumptions are not directly interchangeable.

The demo's common synthetic return matrix makes computed weights comparable on that input; it does not establish an out-of-sample winner. Its Black–Litterman wrapper supplies equal market weights and sample means as views, rather than eliciting independent investor forecasts. The literature guide records the review scope for each reference; the Black–Litterman scan was inspected, but detailed derivations were not independently verified.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Compares multiple optimizer families on one synthetic return matrix. Black–Litterman combines equilibrium information with views. The wrapper assumes equal market weights, sample means as views and tau=1/T; this demo supplies risk aversion rather than explicit investor views. Other branches use Markowitz, Corvalán, smart-beta assumptions and Lai-style resampling. These are separate models, not interchangeable solver settings.

Rolling calibration, rebalance schedules, costs and the dataset used here belong to the demo, not to the static 1952 formulation.

This comparison also includes [Corvalán’s near-efficient diversification framework (2005)](https://www.bcentral.cl/contenido/-/details/documento-de-trabajo-n-336) and [Lai, Xing and Chen’s estimation-risk framework (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-AOAS422). ### How this demo connects to the idea

PortfolioOptimizationAlgorithmDemo.heading: Paper introduction
PortfolioOptimizationAlgorithmDemo.text:
[Tze Leung Lai, Haipeng Xing and Zehao Chen, *Mean–variance portfolio optimization when means and covariances are unknown* (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1214/10-AOAS422) addresses a practical weakness of plug-in mean–variance optimization: historical estimates are uncertain, yet a naive optimizer treats them as known.

The paper formulates allocation using predictive return uncertainty and develops a nonparametric empirical Bayes (NPEB) approach with resampling. Conceptually, the investor should account for estimation risk when evaluating an allocation, rather than optimize once using a single estimated mean and covariance matrix. The method is compared with alternative allocation procedures in numerical and empirical examples.

Its conclusions depend on the statistical modeling and resampling design. The Java API retains `Lai2010`, but the cited journal paper is from 2011. Resampler selection, shrinkage, bootstrap count, risk preference and rebalancing are explicit demo choices, not interchangeable settings guaranteed to reproduce the article's tables. Sections 3–4 of the original text were reviewed.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Builds a composable Lai2010OptimizationAlgorithm with a long-only/shrunk-mean optimizer, Ledoit–Wolf moments and a resampler, then uses getOptimalWeights and a TopN transformation. The selected components and post-processing define an adaptation, not a paper replication.

PortfolioOptimizationBacktestDemo.heading: Paper introduction
PortfolioOptimizationBacktestDemo.text:
[Harry Markowitz, *Portfolio Selection* (1952)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x) explains diversification as a portfolio problem: an asset's risk cannot be judged independently of how its returns move with the other holdings. Expected portfolio return is a weighted mean; portfolio variance depends on the full covariance matrix.

The efficient set contains portfolios for which expected return cannot be improved without accepting more variance, or variance reduced without giving up expected return. An investor selects a tradeoff according to preferences and constraints. Holding many positively correlated assets need not provide much diversification.

The framework assumes the relevant return means and covariances are supplied. In practice, estimates can be unstable and constraints can materially change the answer. A solved optimization is therefore a set of weights under assumptions, not evidence of future outperformance. The original article was reviewed. Rolling calibration, rebalance schedules, costs and the dataset used here belong to the demo, not to the static 1952 formulation.

### How this demo connects to the idea

A rolling backtest separates estimated weights from realized returns after rebalancing. Follow the data-window and rebalance callbacks to see when each estimate is available. Transaction and turnover conventions belong to the simulation, not the static mean–variance equations.

AccumulationDistributionLineDemo.heading: Strategy introduction
AccumulationDistributionLineDemo.text:
This is a technical-indicator tutorial. No single original research paper has been established as the source of this exact demo policy, so the introduction explains its mechanics rather than attributing it to an unverified publication.

An indicator transforms observed price or volume history into a statistic. A strategy adds decisions about when the statistic is available, what constitutes an entry or exit, how large a position to hold and how orders are executed. Those extra choices determine account performance; an indicator series alone is not a backtest.

The recorded run uses the documented synthetic quick-mode inputs, so it teaches the AlgoQuant API rather than measuring a historical market opportunity. Read the specific mechanism below together with the signal, order, simulation and report code. Distinguish periods measured in observations from calendar time and avoid treating parameter tuning on one sample as independent validation.

### How this demo connects to the idea

Accumulation/distribution aggregates volume signed by the close’s location within its high-low range. The demo combines that indicator with smoothed price changes. Its actual target rule, documented above, is an example policy and is not evidence that a divergence signal has positive expected return.

The accumulation/distribution line weights volume by where the close lies within the high–low range and accumulates that signed flow. It is a price/volume indicator, not a direct observation of investor buying and selling.

TutorialStrategyDemo.heading: Strategy introduction
TutorialStrategyDemo.text:
This is an event-driven API lesson rather than a model attributed to a research paper. Its purpose is to show how market data reaches a strategy, how the strategy creates orders and how the simulator records executions and performance.

A complete backtest requires more than a signal formula: data timing, order sizing, fills, account valuation and reporting must agree. Following those components in a small example helps explain how to call the library before introducing a more elaborate statistical model.

The selected rule is instructional. Neither a completed simulator run nor an exported chart validates the rule as an investment strategy. Use the source and observed output to learn the execution lifecycle and identify which assumptions a future production strategy would need to make explicit.

### How this demo connects to the idea

This is an event-handling lesson rather than a published econometric model. Price direction selects a fixed signed-unit target and the existing position determines the incremental order. See TutorialStrategy for equal-price behavior and the companion demo for monthly sampling.

MRModelFixedGridDemo.heading: Strategy introduction
MRModelFixedGridDemo.text:
This example illustrates a mean-reversion or grid-style trading policy assembled in code. No single original publication has been established for the exact rule, so this page explains the strategy without inventing a paper citation.

The broad idea is to change inventory as price moves through configured levels, or as a spread deviates from a reference. Reversals can allow purchases and sales at different levels, while a persistent trend can accumulate exposure or losses. A rule that repeatedly realizes small gains can still carry substantial open-position risk.

The result depends on grid spacing, reference updates, position limits, data frequency, fills and costs. Mean reversion is an assumption to examine, not a property created by the grid itself. Read the implementation below for the exact configuration, and inspect both account value and outstanding inventory when interpreting a simulation.

### How this demo connects to the idea

The fixed-grid variant uses an estimated mean and a grid distance to update a discrete exposure state as the spread diverges or reverts. These are library-specific spread/grid trading policies. A basket converts product prices into a spread; the configured mean-reversion model maps its level or deviation into a desired state, and MeanReversionStrategy translates that state into product orders. Grid distance, periodic/ranged update behavior and scale are distinct controls. The folder name does not mean that option implied volatility is being traded. Mean reversion is an assumption to check, not a property guaranteed by this policy.
